Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 54, verses 9–17:

Before them, the people of Makkah, they denied; they denied Our servant, meaning Nuh (Noah). If you ask: what is the meaning of His saying, "they denied," after His saying, "[the people of Nuh] denied" [[Mahmud said: "If you ask: what is the benefit of 'they denied' after His saying 'the people of Nuh denied before them'...? Ahmad said: His discussion of the saying of the Exalted, 'And those before them denied, and they did not reach a tenth of what We had given them, so they denied My messengers,' has already passed, and he answered it with two answers. One of them is unfeasible here, and the other is possible, namely that it is like the saying of one who says: so-and-so proceeded to disbelief and disbelieved in Muhammad, peace be upon him. Two answers have passed for me: one of them can be applied here, and its summary is the rejection of the question's occurrence, because the first is absolute and the second is restricted, so it is not a repetition. It is like His saying in this surah, 'Then he took up and hamstrung,' for his taking up was itself his hamstringing, but it was mentioned from the aspect of its generality, and then from the aspect of its specificity, as an elaboration, and this is like mentioning it twice. Another answer here: the one who denied first is omitted, indicated by the mention of Nuh, so it is as if He said: the people of Nuh denied Nuh; then He brought their denial a second time, attributed to His saying 'Our servant,' so He described Nuh with the specific quality of servanthood and attributed him to Himself as an attribution of honour. So the denial reported of them a second time is more heinous for them than the one mentioned first, due to that subtle point. And God knows best."]]? I say: its meaning is: they denied, so they denied Our servant, that is, they denied him with denial following denial; whenever a generation of deniers passed away from them, a generation of deniers followed it. Or: the people of Nuh denied the messengers, so they denied Our servant, that is, since they were deniers of the messengers and rejecters of prophethood altogether, they denied Nuh, because he was one of the messengers. "He is mad" — he is mad; "and he was repelled" — they rebuffed him with abuse, beating, and the threat of stoning in their saying, "You will surely be among those stoned." It is also said that it is part of their speech, i.e., they said, "He is mad, and the jinn have repelled him, possessed him, and taken away his mind and carried off his heart." It was read: "Annī" (meaning: so he called out, "I am overcome"), and "Innī" (on the assumption of a saying: so he called and said, "I am overcome" [[His saying "so he called and said, I am overcome" is perhaps: i.e., so he called and said. (Ayn)]]), "my people have overcome me, and they did not listen to me, and despair of their answering me has become firm. So take revenge (fa-ntasir): avenge yourself upon them with a punishment You send against them." He called upon this only after the matter had overwhelmed him and the flood had reached the heights [[His saying "the flood had reached the heights" is perhaps the plural of rabwah, which is what rises from the land like a hillock. Cited from al-Sihah, but there under the letter zay: al-zabiyah is the hillock that water does not rise above. And in the proverb: the flood has reached the zubā. And al-zubyah: a pit dug for the lion in a high place for hunting. End of summary. (Ayn)]]. It is reported that one of his people would meet him and choke him until he fell unconscious. He would then recover, saying, "O God, forgive my people, for they do not know."

It was read: "fa-fataḥnā" lightened and intensified, and likewise "wa-fajjarnā." Ṭuhmar (pouring, unceasing) [mantahir: poured forth in abundance and succession, without stopping for forty days]. "And We caused the earth to gush forth springs": We made the whole earth as if it were springs gushing forth; this is more eloquent than your saying, "and We made the springs of the earth gush forth." Its parallel in composition is "and the head has blazed with grey hair." "Then the waters met": the waters of the sky and of the earth. It was read: "al-māʾān," meaning the two kinds of water, the heavenly and the earthly. Similar to your saying, "I have two dates," meaning two kinds of dates: barni and maʿqili. The poet said:

"For us are two herds of camels, in which is what you know,
So of whichever of them you wish, take up and turn aside."

He says: for us are two herds of camels, in which are the hospitality of guests and the kindness to the poor; so carry whichever of them you wish upon your shoulders, that is, take it and separate it from the rest. Or the meaning: turn away from both and depart from what you intended of them into the sides of the earth, for we are their protectors.

"Ayyuhumā" with a sukūn is a dialect form of the doubled "ayy." "Mā shi'tum" is a substitute for it. It is permissible that "mā" is superfluous, meaning: "fa-fī ayyuhumā shi'tum, fa-nṣarifū fī manākib al-arḍ..." It is permissible that "mā shi'tum" is the object, or an absolute object placed before its governing verb, and the second "fa" is a repetition of the first. It is permissible that it points to the conditional meaning within the governed term, i.e., "fa-immā ʿan ayyihimā"; or "fa-immā mā shi'tum fa-tanakkabū," i.e., avoid them.

Al-Hasan read "al-māwān," changing the hamza to a waw, as in their saying "ʿalbāwān."

"Upon a matter that has been decreed": upon a state which God determined however He willed. It was also said: upon a state that came decreed and equal, namely that the measure of what was sent down from the sky was like the measure of what came forth from the earth, equal in equality. It was also said: upon a matter decreed in the Preserved Tablet that it would occur, namely the destruction of Nuh's people by the flood.

"Upon one of planks and nails": he meant the ship. It is one of the attributes that stand in place of the things described, taking their place and performing their function, without any separation between them and what they describe. Similar to it:

"...but my shirt is a coat of interlinked iron" [the poem: "My saddle is the horse's pommel, but my shirt is interlinked iron." The pommel is the rider's seat on the horse's back. He says: my saddle is my horse's back. "My shirt": a coat of iron of close-woven links, meaning that he is not among the people of luxury but among the people of the desert and raiding. The "but" is of the type of attaching praise with something resembling blame, for the sake of intensified praise.] He meant: "but my shirt is a coat of mail." Likewise:

"And I will surely claim my rights with striving, even if it be in the eyes of the leaping locusts, on their shanks"

He says: there must be striving in securing my rights and taking them, even if they are in the most hidden and remote place, like the eyes of the leaping locusts, springing on their legs (akrāʿ, thin legs; the plural of kurāʿ), so the qualified noun was omitted and referred to by "the leaping ones," its attribute, since it runs in the manner of a noun. It was also said: the meaning is: there must be taking my camels even if they are so emaciated that they are seen in the eyes of the locusts because of their smallness, i.e., even if they were as if they were such.

He meant: "even if it be in the eyes of the locusts." Do you not see that if you combined the ship with this attribute, or the coat of mail with the locusts and these two attributes, it would not be correct? This is from eloquent and wondrous speech. "Dusur" is the plural of dissār, which is the nail, from "dasara," meaning he pushed it, because it is driven through its opening.

"As a recompense" is an object of purpose for what preceded it: the opening of the gates of heaven and what follows, i.e., We did that as a recompense for "him who had been disbelieved," who is Nuh, peace be upon him. He is described as disbelieved because a prophet is a blessing and mercy from God. God the Exalted said, "And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds." So Nuh, peace be upon him, was a disbelieved blessing. From this meaning is what is related: a man said to al-Rashid, "Praise be to God for you," and he said, "What is the meaning of this speech?" He said, "You are a blessing for which I praise God." It is also permissible that it is on the supposition of the omission of the preposition and the connection of the verb.

Qatadah read "kufira," meaning a recompense for the disbelievers. Al-Hasan read "jazā'" with a kasra, meaning requital.

The pronoun in "We left it" refers to the ship, or to the deed, meaning: We made it a sign by which one takes lesson. It is reported from Qatadah: God preserved it in the land of al-Jazirah. It was also said: on al-Judi for a long time, until the first of this community looked at it. "Al-mudakkir" means the one who takes heed. It was read: "mudhtakir," on the original form, and "muddakir," changing the tā' into dhāl and assimilating the dhāl into it. This is like "mudhjir." "Al-nudhur" is the plural of nadhīr, which is the warning.

"And We have certainly made the Qur'an easy for remembrance," meaning: We made it easy for recollection and admonition, by filling it with healing admonitions and turning within it promise and threat, "so is there any who will take heed?" It was also said: We made it easy for memorization and helped whoever wished to memorize it, so is there any seeker of its memorization who will be helped in it. It is also permissible that the meaning is: We prepared it for remembrance, as one says "yassara his she-camel" when he saddles her for travel, and "yassara his horse for the raid" when he saddles and bridles it. The poet said:

"I approached him with the bridle, having prepared him,
There, what I was doing will repay me."

"Ara umm Sahl" etc. [The poem is cited in the commentary as an illustration of the usage of "yassara": "Do you see Umm Sahl does not cease to be grieved? She blames me, and I do not know for what she grieves. She blames me for giving the horse its milk, and the horse and the milk are not equal in the hour of alarm..." The explanation in the text: "al-a'raj" is the outward meaning; "tafajja'" and "tawajja'" have originally two tā's, one of which was dropped for lightness. "'Alām": a question about the cause of grief. "Asnah": to give. "Al-ward" is the name of her horse. "Al-luqḥah": fresh milk. "Al-ḥāsir": woman with uncovered face. "Al-mushmaʿillah": quick in running. "Al-nukhayb": the hollow empty one. The intended meaning is one whose wits and head are gone, "mā yuqni'": that does not cover herself for her bewilderment and shame. His saying "al-ward al-awwal" is the object, and the second is the object with "with"; this describes Umm Sahl's state. As for the state of her mare, it is clarified in his saying: "I approached him, preparing and readying him with the bridle," or "making it easy for him with it," indicating that he was difficult without the bridle. "There" refers to the place of war or its time. "Yajzīnī": gives me as the recompense of my doing with him, and he likened it to one from whom recompense can be valid, by way of metaphor. "Ṣun'ī" is his giving her milk.]

It is also related that the books of the religions, such as the Torah and the Gospel, were not recited by their people except by looking into them, and they did not memorize them outwardly as the Qur'an is memorized.

Warnings. And My warning to them of the punishment before it descended; or a warning that came through their destruction to those after them.

On a day of misfortune (nahs), meaning an ill-omened day. It was also read as "yawman nahisan," like His saying "in days of ill omen" (ayyamin nahisat).

Continuous (mustamirr): it persisted over them and lasted until it destroyed them. Or it persisted over them all, both their greatest and least, until not a single soul of them remained. It was a Wednesday at the end of the month, which does not recur.

It is also permissible that by "mustamirr" is meant: extremely bitter and hideous.

It uproots people (tanzi'u al-nas): it pulls them up (tuqli'uhum) from their places. They used to line up, taking each other's hands with one another's hands [[The phrase "taking each other's hands with one another's hands" is the wording of al-Nasafi: "taking some of them by the hands of others." (Gh.)

.]].

They would enter the ravines and dig pits, sinking into them; then it would uproot them, overturn them, and break their necks. ﴿As if they were trunks of hollow palm trees﴾ (a'jaz nakhlin munqa'ir). He means that they were falling to the ground dead, while they were tall, massive bodies, ﴿as if they were trunks of palm trees﴾, meaning their roots without branches. Munqa'ir means uprooted from its place of planting. It is also said: they were likened to palm trunks because the wind would cut off their heads, leaving bodies without heads.

He described the palm with the masculine form (naklin) according to the wording; had He treated it according to meaning, He would have used the feminine, as in His saying ﴿a'jaz nakhlin khawiyah﴾ (trunks of hollow palm trees).

*"As a trial for them"* — a test and an affliction for them. *"So watch them"* — wait for them and observe what they will do. *"And be patient"* — endure their harm and do not hasten until My command comes to you.

*"Present"* — present, attended, for them or for the she-camel. It is also said: they attend the water on their turn, and the milk on her turn.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 54, verse 33–40:

Ḥāṣiban (a violent wind), "rīḥan tuḥṣibuhum bil-ḥijārah" [﴿a wind that pelts them with stones﴾]. That is: it strikes them with stones at saḥar (the last part of the night). It is said that the saḥar is the last sixth of it. It was also said: there are two saḥars, the upper saḥar, before the breaking of dawn, and the other at its breaking. He recited:

"Marrat bi-aʿlā s-saḥrayn tadhʾal — yā sāʾilī in kunta ʿanhā tasʾal"
[She passed by the upper of the two saḥars, hastening — O you who ask me, if you ask about them...]

He says: O you who asks me, if you ask about the wild asses only, they passed by the upper saḥar, which is the saḥar before the breaking of dawn. The lower one is the one at its breaking. That is, she passed in the first saḥar, tadhʾal, with a hamza, meaning: she hastened in walking, from dhaʾala (like manaʿa), when one walks lightly. From this comes dhuʾālat al-dhiʾb (the quick gait of the wolf). Between tasʾal and tadhʾal there is the paronomasia of the imperfect (al-jinās al-muḍāriʿ).

[It is declined (ṣuriff) because it is indefinite (nakira). It is said: "I met him saḥar," if you met him in the saḥar of his day.] Niʿmatan (as a blessing), an object of purpose (mafʿūl lahu): "mantashakara niʿmatallāhi bi-īmānihi wa ṭāʿatihi" [﴿for a favour from Us. Thus We reward those who are grateful﴾]. "Wa laqad anḏarahum" [﴿And he had warned them﴾], Lot, peace be upon him, "baṭshatanā" [﴿Our assault﴾], Our seizing them with punishment. "Fatamāraw" [﴿So they disputed﴾], they denied the warnings, one doubting the other. "Fa-ṭamasnā aʿyunahum" [﴿Then We obliterated their eyes﴾], We wiped them out and made them like the rest of the face, with no slit visible. It is related that when they tried to force the door of Lot, peace be upon him, to enter, the angels said: "Let them enter," "innā rusulu rabbika lan yaṣilū ilayka" [﴿We are messengers of your Lord; they will never reach you﴾]. So Gabriel, peace be upon him, struck them with his wing, a single blow, and left them groping, unable to find the door, until Lot brought them out. "Fa-dhūqū" [﴿So taste﴾], I said to them, through the tongues of the angels: "bukrah" [﴿morning﴾], early in the day, and at dawn, like His saying: "mushriqīn" [﴿at sunrise﴾] and "muṣbiḥīn" [﴿in the morning﴾].

Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "bukratan" without tanwīn (nunation), as a diptote: you say "ataytuhu bukrah" and "ghadwah" with tanwīn when you intend indefiniteness, and without it when you define it and mean the morning of your day or its early part. "ʿAdhābun mustaqirr" [﴿a settled punishment﴾], established, firmly fixed upon them until it leads them to the punishment of the Hereafter. If you ask: what is the benefit of repeating "fa-dhūqū ʿadhābī wa nudhur" and "wa laqad yassarnā al-Qurʾāna li-l-dhikri fa-hal min muddakir?" I say: its benefit is that they renew, each time they hear a report of the tidings of the earlier peoples, remembrance and admonition, and that they resume alertness and awakening when they hear the exhortation to that and the urging toward it; and that the staff be struck for them repeatedly, and the waterskin be rattled for them at intervals, lest forgetfulness overcome them and heedlessness take hold of them. Such is the wisdom of repetition, as in His saying: "fa-bi-ayyi ālāʾi rabbikumā tukadhdhibān" [﴿So which of the favours of your Lord would you deny?﴾] at every blessing He enumerates in Surat al-Raḥmān, and His saying: "fa-waylun yawmaʾidhin lil-mukadhdhibīn" [﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾] at every verse He mentions in Surat al-Mursalāt. Likewise the repetition of reports and stories in themselves, so that those lessons remain present in hearts, impressed upon minds, and remembered, not forgotten, at every time.

"We are a united multitude (jami') victorious (muntasir), a collective (mujtami') that cannot be overcome, unassailable and unassailed." It is narrated from Abu Jahl that on the day of Badr he struck his horse, advanced in the ranks and said: "Today we will avenge ourselves on Muhammad and his companions." Then when he saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) leaping in his armour and saying: "The multitude will be routed," he understood its interpretation. Saqar is a proper name for Hell. It is derived from "saqarathu al-nar" and "saqarathu," meaning that it scorched him when it burned him. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"When the sun melts, he guards against its scorching
with the branches of a rain-watered, leafy tree on a sandy dune."

[Dhu al-Rummah describes wild cattle. It is said that the sun "melts" (dhābat al-shams) when its heat intensifies until something drips from its rays like saliva. Ṣaqara al-ṣakhra bi-l-miṣqar means he struck the rock with a pickaxe to break it. Ṣaqarathu al-shams means the sun struck him and changed his colour. Ṣaqrat al-shams means the intensity of the sun's blow on the ground. Al-afnān is the plural of fanan, the dense, intertwined foliage gathered on a branch.

Al-marbūʿ is that which has been struck by spring rain. Al-ṣarīmah is the sandy dune that breaks off from the sands. Al-muʿabbal is abundant in leaves and luxuriant.

He says: when the sun's heat intensifies, he protects himself from its severity with branches of a tree watered by spring in this sandy place. Al-muʿabbal means abundant in leaves. Muʿabbal is a substitute (badal) for marbūʿ, as if it were a noun in apposition. It is also permissible that it is an adjective for it, in which case its annexation is an annexation of description to a time or place, which does not give definiteness, so it is valid to describe it with an indefinite noun.]

﴿Indeed, We created everything by measure﴾: the word "kulla" (everything) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that the apparent verb explains. Its non-declension is due to definiteness and feminine form.

[Mahmud said: "It is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb that the apparent verb explains." Ahmad said: The analogy of what the grammarians established would be to prefer the nominative for "kull," but none of the seven readers recited it that way. It was so because with the nominative the speech is one sentence, and with the accusative it is two sentences, and the nominative is more concise. Moreover, there is no requirement for the accusative here from any of the six categories, namely the imperative, the prohibition... to the end of the list, and I find here no conjunction or other thing that they count among the grounds for choosing the accusative. Once this is clear, know that he turned away from the nominative by ijmāʿ (scholarly consensus) for a subtle reason that determines the choice of the accusative: if it were nominative, the clause "We created him" would fall as a description of a thing, and the phrase "bi-qadar" would be an information (khabar) about every thing qualified by the description, and the sentence would come to mean: "Indeed every created thing is for Us by measure." This would imply that a created thing attributed to other than God is not by measure. But on the accusative the sentence becomes: "Indeed We created every thing by measure," which conveys the generality of every created thing's relation to God Most High. Since this benefit is not matched by the verbal benefit of the nominative reading, along with the deficiency of meaning in the nominative, and since in this widely transmitted reading the meaning comes out complete and clear like the dawn, they unanimously agreed to turn away from the nominative to the accusative. However, Zamakhshari, since it was the principle of his school to divide created things into God's creation and things created for others, saying "this is for God, in their claim, this is for us," this verse struck him, and the consensus of the readers stood as proof against him. So he began to seek comfort in the wretchedness, and to transmit its reading in the nominative. Let him consult and be shown the withdrawal of the seven readers from this report, though it is the preferred form in Arabic, were it not for what we have mentioned. Is it permissible, in his judgment, then, to hold consensus upon what is less preferred in wording and meaning, without any meaning requiring that? Or not? He is the one who decides what he judges. To God return all matters.]

However, Zamakhshari, since it was the principle of his school to divide created things into God's creation and things created for others, saying "this is for God, in their claim, this is for us," this verse struck him, and the consensus of the readers stood as proof against him. So he began to seek comfort in the wretchedness, and to transmit its reading in the nominative. Let him consult and be shown the withdrawal of the seven readers from this report, though it is the preferred form in Arabic, were it not for what we have mentioned. Is it permissible, in his judgment, then, to hold consensus upon what is less preferred in wording and meaning, without any meaning requiring that? Or not? He is the one who decides what he judges. To God return all matters.]
